title: Identify Equivalent Algebraic Expressions
objective: I can show that two expressions are equivalent by simplifying and combining like terms.
model: two expressions with the same value for every substitution: collect like terms, and test with two numbers (algebra tiles to see 3x + 2x as 5 x-tiles)

widgets.component: Insert Coin: 4n + 3 at n = 5, '7 more than x', 9t, 30 − 4y at y = 6
widgets.root: The lesson's warm-up (6-5 review); keys 23, x + 7, 9t, 6 recomputed.

widgets.component: 4x + 3x and 5n + 2n equivalent forms
widgets.root: Combine like terms is the objective; wrong choices 7x², 12x, 43x name the exponent, multiply and concatenate slips.

widgets.component: Equivalent to 2(m + 5); which property is 3(x + 7) = 3x + 21; 'Spot the Distributive Mistake'
widgets.root: The distributive property a(b + c) = ab + ac, with expanding and factoring, is derived in 6-14 (area-model lesson) and combining after distributing in 6-15; nothing earlier in Unit 6 teaches it (6-6's own config lists it in the key idea and in two approaching items, so the conflict starts in the lesson text). The err card and hints teach 'multiply BOTH terms', and 2.3 asks the student to name the property.
widgets.replacement: Move these three to the 6-14 studio. Replace with like-terms items: 2.2 'Which expression is equivalent to 7m − 3m + 2?' (4m + 2), 2.3 'Which statement shows why 2x + 3x = 5x? x-tiles: 2 + 3 = 5 tiles' (choose the tile picture/sentence), 2.5 err 'Maya wrote 4x + 3x = 7x²' (squared the variable).

widgets.component: Match six expressions to their simplified equivalents (6x + 2x, 3(n + 5), 4a + 7 + a, 2(3y − 4), 10m − 4m + 1, 5(x + 2))
widgets.root: Three of the six pairs (3(n + 5) → 3n + 15, 2(3y − 4) → 6y − 8, 5(x + 2) → 5x + 10) require expanding a product over a sum, which is 6-14 content; the other three are right for this lesson.
widgets.replacement: Keep 6x + 2x → 8x, 4a + 7 + a → 5a + 7, 10m − 4m + 1 → 6m + 1 and replace the other three pairs with 9 + 2n + 5 → 2n + 14, 8y − 3y → 5y, n + n + n + 4 → 3n + 4.

widgets.component: Original → Simplified → value at x = 3 for 2x + 5x + 1, 4(x + 2), 3x + 4 + x − 1
widgets.root: The 'Simplified' column is free text compared as a string ('7x + 1', '4x + 8', '4x + 3'): '7x+1' with no spaces, '1 + 7x' or '7 x + 1' are all marked wrong, and the input is inputmode=decimal (no letters on a tablet keypad). The middle row also needs the distributive property.
widgets.replacement: Replace the typed column with a one-choice select per row (four candidate expressions) and keep the numeric 'value when x = 3' column (22, 20, 15 grade by value); swap row 2 for 6n + 3 + n − 1 → 7n + 2. In K.tbl normalise whitespace before comparing as a safety net.

widgets.component: Spot the Combining Mistake: 'combine every number you see' → 7x + 3 + 2x = 12x
widgets.root: The slip (adding coefficients, variable-free constants and 9x together) is the lesson's central like-terms misconception, at the right step.

widgets.component: Generated 'which expression is equivalent', 'always true', 'not equivalent' with sums, products over sums and substitution tests
widgets.root: Measured over 300 draws per level, 26% of L1, 58% of L2 and 83% of L3 stems need distributing (6(b + 5) → 6b + 30, 7(w − 3) → 7w − 21, 2b + 6 = 2(b + 3), 4(t + 6) + t); The distributive property a(b + c) = ab + ac, with expanding and factoring, is derived in 6-14 (area-model lesson) and combining after distributing in 6-15; nothing earlier in Unit 6 teaches it (6-6's own config lists it in the key idea and in two approaching items, so the conflict starts in the lesson text).
widgets.replacement: Restrict equivalentExpr when called from 6-6 to its like-terms and commutative subtypes (param noDistribute): L1 'equivalent to 8n + 6n', L2 'equivalent to 2d + 3 + 4d' and 'always true: 7 + 7t = 7t + 7', L3 'three are equivalent to 6d + 2 + d + 6, which is not'. Keep the distributive subtypes for the 6-14 studio.

widgets.component: Algebra tiles: build tiles for an expression equivalent to 4(2x + 1)
widgets.root: Equivalent mode asks for k(ax + b) with k = 2-4 ('Build tiles for an expression equivalent to 3(2x + 6)'): the tile model of distribution, i.e. the 6-14 lesson's area model, used eight lessons early.
widgets.replacement: Use act:tiles mode combine L2 here ('Combine the like terms in 2x + 5 + x − 3': tap like tiles to group, type the shorter expression) and move equivalent mode to 6-14.

widgets.component: Are the two pricing formulas equivalent? / what does each expression equal when h = 5?
widgets.root: Connect.check items 2-3 lifted without the scenario (Client A pays 4h + 2h + 30, Client B pays 6h + 30) or its tape diagram; 5.3 refers to 'A' and 'B' that are never defined, so 'A = 60 and B = 55' cannot be evaluated.
widgets.replacement: Prefix both stems: 'A music studio charges Client A 4h + 2h + 30 dollars for h hours and Client B 6h + 30 dollars.' Keep keys (Yes; both 60 at h = 5) and attach the 'Two Fair Studio Prices' tape diagram.

widgets.root: The objective itself; recomputed 2r + 2, 5a + 9, 3k + 12; distractors name coefficient multiplication, squaring, concatenation.

widgets.component: 'Noor says 5w + 1 and 2w + 16 are not equivalent. Which reasoning proves Noor is right?'
widgets.root: Two choices are defensible: 'Try w = 7: 36 and 30. One test is not enough to decide' is false (one value that gives different results already proves the expressions are not equivalent), and the key 'try w = 5: both 26, then w = 7: 36 and 30' has to open with a decoy test that matches. The item teaches that a counterexample needs company.
widgets.replacement: Rewrite the L4 equivalentExpr stem as 'Which test PROVES the two expressions are not equivalent?': key 'Try w = 7: 36 and 30. The values differ, so they are not equivalent.' Distractors: 'Try w = 5: both are 26, so they are equivalent' (one match proves nothing), 'They look different so they are not equivalent', 'Try w = 7 and w = 7 again'. Remove the 'one test is not enough' option when the test gives different values.
